screens.title: What is Foundry?
screens.narratorSegment: Foundry is a toolkit written in Rust that brings compilation, testing, scripting, and blockchain interaction into a fast, lightweight CLI workflow. Define it plainly: Foundry bundles Forge for compile and test tasks, Cast for command-line EVM interactions, and Anvil as a local node. The key claim is that Foundry is Solidity-first. That means you can write tests and deployment scripts in Solidity itself instead of switching to JavaScript. A concrete example: instead of writing a JavaScript deploy script that imports ethers and constructs transactions, you author a Solidity contract that implements run(), call vm. startBroadcast(), and deploy contracts with new. This reduces context switching for Solidity developers and often improves speed. A common misconception is that Solidity scripting removes the need for off-chain logic; it does not. If you need complex off-chain orchestration, JS tooling remains useful. The takeaway is practical: when your team prefers Solidity for testing and deployment logic, Foundry offers a consistent, fast environment that keeps your deployment code in the same language as your contracts. Which parts of your current workflow would simplify by staying in Solidity?

Core Concept
What is Foundry?
Foundry bundles tools that are fast and let you write tests and scripts in Solidity.
  • Forge — compile, test, and run scripts.
  • Cast — command-line calls and transactions.
  • Anvil — local Ethereum node for development.
Analogy
Think of Foundry as a minimal toolbelt: the razor-sharp Rust core performs the heavy lifting while you script in Solidity.
Concrete example
// Example pattern described in prose: a Solidity script contract inherits from Script.sol,
// uses vm.startBroadcast() to begin signing transactions, then deploys via new ContractName().
Misconception: Solidity scripting removes need for off-chain tasks. Contrast: some orchestration still belongs off-chain.
Key Takeaway

Foundry keeps build and deploy logic close to your contracts, reducing context switching and improving performance.

screens.title: Foundry's Components
screens.narratorSegment: Foundry is intentionally modular. Forge is the developer-facing tool for compiling, testing, and running Solidity scripts. Cast is a small but powerful CLI that lets you call view functions and send transactions from the terminal. Anvil provides a fast local chain for testing, similar in purpose to other local nodes but designed for speed. A concrete workflow: you run Anvil to get a local chain, use forge test to run Solidity tests against it, author a script inheriting from Script. sol and call vm helpers, then use forge script to simulate and optionally broadcast with a real RPC. Cast then lets you query the same chain for view results or sign transactions with a private key. A common confusion is to think Cast replaces a scripting language; it does not. Cast is for single-command interactions and quick checks. The visual above maps components and their common commands, so you can see how a command like forge script connects to RPCs while cast is used for ad-hoc calls. Which component will you reach for first when iterating on a contract? Foundry's Components means forge runs and deploys scripts, cast interacts via cli, anvil is the local chain. combine them for development and deployment.. In practical terms, forge, cast, and anvil — roles and interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition
Forge · Cast · Anvil
Forge
Compile, test, run scripts. Use forge init and forge script to manage files and deployments.
Example commands:
forge init my-foundry-project
forge script script/Deploy.s.sol:Deploy --rpc-url $RPC --broadcast
Cast
Call view functions and send transactions without a full script. Ideal for quick checks and reads.
Example commands:
cast call <ADDRESS> "greet()(string)" --rpc-url $RPC

Anvil
A local node for fast, isolated development. Run Anvil to test scripts and transactions locally before targeting live networks.
Why it matters
Use Anvil to iterate quickly without spending testnet gas and to inspect state locally.

screens.title: Install and Initialize Foundry
screens.narratorSegment: Getting started with Foundry is a short terminal-first process. First, install Foundry using foundryup, which sets up Forge, Cast, and Anvil in your environment. This single installer ensures the Rust-native binaries are available. As a concrete step, run foundryup once, then use forge init followed by the project name to scaffold folders and example files. When you run forge init my-foundry-project you will see src, lib, script, and test directories created. The src folder is where contracts belong. The script folder is where Forge deployment scripts live. The lib directory is for third-party libraries, often added with forge install. A common misconception is that forge init populates all dependencies; it creates the skeleton and example files only. You still need to install OpenZeppelin or other libraries with forge install. After initializing, check your project structure and consider adding. gitignore entries for secrets. The practical takeaway: install once with foundryup, scaffold with forge init, and then add libraries and environment variables before attempting a live deployment. screens.title: Project Structure and Files
screens.narratorSegment: A predictable project structure avoids confusion and makes automation easier. Foundry projects initialized with forge init create four folders by convention: src for your smart contracts, script for Forge deployment scripts, lib for third-party dependencies installed via forge install, and test for Solidity-based tests. The src folder holds contract code like Greeter or MyNFT. Script contains deployment scripts such as DeployGreeter. s. sol that inherit Script. sol and implement run(). The lib folder should contain libraries such as OpenZeppelin when installed. Tests written in Solidity live in test and interoperate with Forge's test runner. A typical workflow is to author contracts in src, add libraries to lib, write tests in test, and add deployment logic in script. A common misunderstanding is assuming scripts run automatically on compilation; they do not. You must explicitly call forge script with the script path and target. The practical habit: keep one contract per file in src and keep scripts focused on deployment steps with clear vm. startBroadcast and vm. stopBroadcast boundaries. screens.title: Forge Scripts in Solidity
screens.narratorSegment: Forge scripts are Solidity contracts that inherit from Script. sol and implement a run function. The run function is executed by forge script. Inside run you mark the point where transactions should be signed by calling vm. startBroadcast and later call vm. stopBroadcast to stop sending signed transactions. A concrete example is deploying a Greeter contract: inside run you start broadcasting, deploy with new Greeter, and stop broadcasting. The vm helpers offer direct control over EVM state and transaction signing from within Solidity. One important behavior to understand is simulation versus broadcast: forge script can execute in simulation mode without --broadcast, which helps test flows without sending transactions. A common mistake is forgetting the --broadcast flag when you intend to deploy to a live network; without it you only simulate. Another subtle point is key sourcing: Foundry uses FOUNDRY_PRIVATE_KEY or CLI flags to sign. The practical skill is to write concise deployment scripts that bracket state-changing operations with vm. startBroadcast and vm. stopBroadcast, verify locally, then run with --broadcast when ready. How will you structure your scripts to minimize risk?

keyIdea.text: A Forge script implements run(), uses vm.startBroadcast() and vm.stopBroadcast(), and is executed with forge script.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Forge scripts in Solidity
Scripts inherit Script.sol and use vm helpers to control broadcasting.
// script/DeployGreeter.s.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import "forge-std/Script.sol";
import "../src/Greeter.sol";

contract DeployGreeter is Script {
  function run() public returns (Greeter greeter) {
    // Start broadcasting transactions from the configured deployer
    vm.startBroadcast();

    greeter = new Greeter("Hello, Foundry!");

    vm.stopBroadcast();
  }
}
Explanation & pitfalls
  • vm.startBroadcast marks when transactions are signed and sent.
  • Without --broadcast, forge script only simulates actions locally.
  • Private keys are read from FOUNDRY_PRIVATE_KEY or CLI args; never hardcode keys.
Pro Tip
Simulate with high verbosity before broadcasting; use -vvvv to inspect transaction steps.

keyIdea.text: Deploy Greeter by writing a Solidity script that calls vm.startBroadcast, creates the contract, and calls vm.stopBroadcast.

content.html:
Contract
Greeter stores and returns a greeting string. Below is the contract source as used in the example.
// src/Greeter.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

contract Greeter {
  string private _greeting;

  constructor(string memory greeting_) { _greeting = greeting_; }

  function greet() public view returns (string memory) { return _greeting; }

  function setGreeting(string memory greeting_) public { _greeting = greeting_; }
}
Deployment Script
This script demonstrates the vm.startBroadcast pattern and logs the deployed address.
// script/DeployGreeter.s.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import "forge-std/Script.sol";
import "../src/Greeter.sol";

contract DeployGreeter is Script {
  function run() public returns (Greeter greeter) {

  }
}

The critical flag when you want to send transactions is --broadcast. Without that flag Forge only simulates the script. Another flag you will use often is --verify to attempt source verification after deployment, which requires an A P I key for the target explorer. Use -vvvv to enable verbose logs that show calldata and gas estimates — that helps debug reverts or gas failures. If you forget --broadcast you will see simulation output but no on-chain transaction. Also consider gas-price or priority-gas-price flags if you need to control gas behavior. screens.title: Common Mistakes & Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson focuses on recurring errors and safety practices when deploying with Foundry. The first and most common mistake is omitting the --broadcast flag: forge script without broadcast only simulates the script locally. If you expected an on-chain deployment and forgot the flag, you will see simulated success but no contract on the network. Second, environment misconfiguration—incorrect FOUNDRY_PRIVATE_KEY or RPC URL—can prevent transactions from being signed or sent. Always confirm your account is funded and the RPC is reachable. Third, gas issues: low balances or incorrect gas configuration can cause transaction failures. You can supply gas-price or priority-gas-price to control behavior. Fourth, security of private keys: never hardcode keys. Use environment variables or keystore files. A contrast to remember: JavaScript-based flows often keep keys in tools like ethers. js; Foundry reads the key from env or CLI. The final checklist: simulate first, verify env vars, ensure funding, then broadcast. After that, check the on-chain address and verify source if needed. screens.title: Foundry vs Hardhat
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing Foundry and Hardhat helps you choose the tool that matches your team's skills. Foundry is Rust-native and pushes a Solidity-first approach: tests and scripts can be written in Solidity, which reduces context switching for Solidity developers. Hardhat is JavaScript-first, offering a rich plugin ecosystem and tight editor integrations for JavaScript and TypeScript developers. In practice, Foundry often offers faster test and compile cycles due to its Rust performance. A concrete contrast: a developer comfortable writing deployment logic in JavaScript might prefer Hardhat for its ecosystem, while a developer who wants to keep deployment logic inside Solidity benefits from Foundry's Script. sol approach and vm helpers. Debugging differs too: Hardhat integrates into some editors with interactive debuggers, while Foundry provides CLI tools such as forge debug. The common misconception is that one tool is strictly superior; the right choice depends on team expertise, the need for plugins, and preference for Solidity-first scripting. fullNarratorScript:
Foundry is a Rust-based toolkit designed to keep Solidity developers working in Solidity. In this lesson you will learn why Foundry matters, what its three core tools do, and how deploying with Forge differs from JS-based workflows. We will show concrete commands and short scripts so you can initialize a project, write a Solidity deployment script that uses the vm helpers, and actually send transactions to Sepolia. You will also learn to use Cast for command-line interaction and common safety checks to avoid simulation-only runs. The goal is to make you comfortable creating a new Foundry project, writing a simple deployment script, and verifying or interacting with the deployed contract. By the end, you will know which environment variables to set, what the --broadcast flag does, and how to query deployed contracts from the terminal. Keep an eye out for common mistakes like forgetting to broadcast transactions and for guidance on private key safety. Ready to see how a Solidity-first deployment flow fits into your toolchain?

In this chapter you will set up a new Foundry project, author deployment scripts in Solidity, and interact with deployed contracts from the command line. First, you will initialize a project scaffold with forge init so you have src, lib, script, and test folders ready for contracts and scripts. Second, you will learn Foundry’s three components: Forge for compiling and deploying, Cast for CLI interaction, and Anvil as a local node. Third, you will write Forge deployment scripts that inherit from Script. sol and use vm. startBroadcast and vm. stopBroadcast to sign and send transactions. Finally, you will practice querying and sending transactions with Cast calls and sends. Each objective includes a practical reason: initialization prevents structural mistakes, understanding the components helps you choose the right tool for a task, scripting in Solidity reduces context switching, and Cast ensures fast, repeatable interactions from the terminal. These skills make deployments safer and more reproducible in team settings. Which objective is most relevant to your next project?

These objectives translate directly into practical tasks you will perform. First, initializing a Foundry project gives you a predictable layout so deployment scripts and tests remain discoverable. As a concrete example, running forge init creates src for contracts and script for deployment logic. Second, understanding Forge, Cast, and Anvil helps you choose whether to run a local node or target a testnet. For example, use Anvil for fast, isolated testing during development, and use forge script with an RPC URL to deploy to Sepolia. Third, writing scripts in Solidity reduces context switching; you will compile and run the same language your contracts use, and vm. startBroadcast marks the point when transactions are signed and sent. Fourth, Cast lets you quickly call view functions or send transactions without writing extra scripts. Each objective matters because it decreases friction and improves reproducibility. As you move through the chapter, think about which practical task you need next and match it to the objective that enables it.

Foundry is a toolkit written in Rust that brings compilation, testing, scripting, and blockchain interaction into a fast, lightweight CLI workflow. Define it plainly: Foundry bundles Forge for compile and test tasks, Cast for command-line EVM interactions, and Anvil as a local node. The key claim is that Foundry is Solidity-first. That means you can write tests and deployment scripts in Solidity itself instead of switching to JavaScript. A concrete example: instead of writing a JavaScript deploy script that imports ethers and constructs transactions, you author a Solidity contract that implements run(), call vm. startBroadcast(), and deploy contracts with new. This reduces context switching for Solidity developers and often improves speed. A common misconception is that Solidity scripting removes the need for off-chain logic; it does not. If you need complex off-chain orchestration, JS tooling remains useful. The takeaway is practical: when your team prefers Solidity for testing and deployment logic, Foundry offers a consistent, fast environment that keeps your deployment code in the same language as your contracts. Which parts of your current workflow would simplify by staying in Solidity?

Foundry is intentionally modular. Forge is the developer-facing tool for compiling, testing, and running Solidity scripts. Cast is a small but powerful CLI that lets you call view functions and send transactions from the terminal. Anvil provides a fast local chain for testing, similar in purpose to other local nodes but designed for speed. A concrete workflow: you run Anvil to get a local chain, use forge test to run Solidity tests against it, author a script inheriting from Script. sol and call vm helpers, then use forge script to simulate and optionally broadcast with a real RPC. Cast then lets you query the same chain for view results or sign transactions with a private key. A common confusion is to think Cast replaces a scripting language; it does not. Cast is for single-command interactions and quick checks. The visual above maps components and their common commands, so you can see how a command like forge script connects to RPCs while cast is used for ad-hoc calls. Which component will you reach for first when iterating on a contract? Getting started with Foundry is a short terminal-first process. First, install Foundry using foundryup, which sets up Forge, Cast, and Anvil in your environment. This single installer ensures the Rust-native binaries are available. As a concrete step, run foundryup once, then use forge init followed by the project name to scaffold folders and example files. When you run forge init my-foundry-project you will see src, lib, script, and test directories created. The src folder is where contracts belong. The script folder is where Forge deployment scripts live. The lib directory is for third-party libraries, often added with forge install. A common misconception is that forge init populates all dependencies; it creates the skeleton and example files only. You still need to install OpenZeppelin or other libraries with forge install. The src folder holds contract code like Greeter or MyNFT. Script contains deployment scripts such as DeployGreeter. s. sol that inherit Script. sol and implement run(). The lib folder should contain libraries such as OpenZeppelin when installed. Tests written in Solidity live in test and interoperate with Forge's test runner. Inside run you mark the point where transactions should be signed by calling vm. startBroadcast and later call vm. stopBroadcast to stop sending signed transactions. This lesson focuses on recurring errors and safety practices when deploying with Foundry. The first and most common mistake is omitting the --broadcast flag: forge script without broadcast only simulates the script locally. If you expected an on-chain deployment and forgot the flag, you will see simulated success but no contract on the network. Second, environment misconfiguration—incorrect FOUNDRY_PRIVATE_KEY or RPC URL—can prevent transactions from being signed or sent. Always confirm your account is funded and the RPC is reachable. Third, gas issues: low balances or incorrect gas configuration can cause transaction failures. You can supply gas-price or priority-gas-price to control behavior. Fourth, security of private keys: never hardcode keys. Use environment variables or keystore files. A contrast to remember: JavaScript-based flows often keep keys in tools like ethers. js; Foundry reads the key from env or CLI. The final checklist: simulate first, verify env vars, ensure funding, then broadcast. After that, check the on-chain address and verify source if needed. Comparing Foundry and Hardhat helps you choose the tool that matches your team's skills. Foundry is Rust-native and pushes a Solidity-first approach: tests and scripts can be written in Solidity, which reduces context switching for Solidity developers. Hardhat is JavaScript-first, offering a rich plugin ecosystem and tight editor integrations for JavaScript and TypeScript developers. In practice, Foundry often offers faster test and compile cycles due to its Rust performance. A concrete contrast: a developer comfortable writing deployment logic in JavaScript might prefer Hardhat for its ecosystem, while a developer who wants to keep deployment logic inside Solidity benefits from Foundry's Script. sol approach and vm helpers. Debugging differs too: Hardhat integrates into some editors with interactive debuggers, while Foundry provides CLI tools such as forge debug. The common misconception is that one tool is strictly superior; the right choice depends on team expertise, the need for plugins, and preference for Solidity-first scripting. The takeaway: evaluate your project's needs and pick the workflow that minimizes context switching and maximizes productivity for your team.
